title: Which substrate reacts fastest
asks: Several alkyl halides are listed. Pick the one that reacts fastest (or slowest) by the mechanism named.

know.h: {{SN2}} order: methyl > primary > secondary >>> tertiary (no {{SN2}}). Steric hindrance slows the approaching nucleophile, which must reach the back of the carbon that carries the leaving group.
The lecture's {{SN2}} numbers, to memorize: allyl 1.3; methyl 1; ethyl 0.033; isobutyl 0.003; isopropyl 0.00083; tert-butyl 0; vinyl 0.
Allyl ({{CH2=CHCH2-LG}}, leaving group on the {{sp3}} carbon next to a C=C) is faster than methyl in {{SN2}}: the neighbouring pi bond stabilizes the transition state.

Vinyl ({{CH2=CH-LG}}, leaving group on a carbon of the C=C) does not react by {{SN2}} (the back of an {{sp2}} carbon cannot be reached) or by {{SN1}} (a vinyl cation is too unstable). The same holds for a leaving group on a benzene ring.

Isobutyl, {{(CH3)2CHCH2-LG}}, is primary but branched on the next carbon: 0.003, ten times slower than ethyl and still faster than isopropyl (0.00083). More branching next door (three methyl groups) is slower again.
{{SN1}} order: tertiary > secondary; primary and methyl do not react by {{SN1}}. Allyl does; vinyl does not. The slow step makes a carbocation, so the rate follows carbocation stability.
Resonance stabilizes a carbocation: an allylic cation shares its positive charge between two carbons, so an allylic halide ionizes faster than the matching halide without the double bond.

{{E2}} order: tertiary > secondary > primary. The transition state is becoming an alkene, and more substituted alkenes are more stable. Branching on the alpha and beta carbons favours {{E2}} over {{SN2}}.
{{E2}} needs a beta hydrogen: a hydrogen on the carbon next to the one that carries the leaving group. A methyl halide has none, and neither does a compound such as {{(CH3)3CCH2Br}}.
Skill: classify a carbon as methyl, primary, secondary or tertiary by counting the carbons attached to the carbon that carries the leaving group, in chains and in rings.
Skill: tell allyl from vinyl and benzyl from aryl by finding exactly which carbon carries the leaving group and whether it is {{sp3}} or {{sp2}}.

method: Read the mechanism named ({{SN2}}, {{SN1}} or {{E2}}) and whether the question asks for the fastest or the slowest.
In each compound find the carbon that carries the leaving group and classify it: methyl, primary, secondary, tertiary, allyl, or vinyl/aryl.
Cross out the compounds that cannot react by that mechanism: tertiary and vinyl for {{SN2}}; methyl, primary and vinyl for {{SN1}}; no beta hydrogen for {{E2}}.
Apply the order for the mechanism: {{SN2}} by sterics (allyl > methyl > primary > secondary), {{SN1}} and {{E2}} by substitution (tertiary > secondary > primary).
If two compounds are in the same class, look at branching on the next carbon ({{SN2}}) or at resonance in the carbocation ({{SN1}}).
Check your choice against the lecture's numbers and against the word fastest or slowest in the question.

pitfalls.h: Using the {{SN1}} order for an {{SN2}} question, or the reverse. They are opposite: tertiary is zero in {{SN2}} and best in {{SN1}}.
Confusing allyl (1.3, the fastest {{SN2}} substrate, and able to do {{SN1}}) with vinyl (0 for both).
Answering fastest when the question asks for slowest.
Treating all primary halides as equal, or placing isobutyl (0.003) below isopropyl (0.00083) because it has more carbons.
Picking the most branched compound for {{E2}} without checking that it has a hydrogen on the next carbon.
